feeConfigTreasuries.note: FIXED. FeeConfig originally stored the treasury *owner* wallets below, but release_escrow/execute_dispute_outcome require each treasury to deserialize as a Token-2022 TokenAccount — and those wallet addresses did not exist on chain at all, so the entire release path was unexecutable on devnet. The escrow program gained an admin-gated `update_fee_config` (which takes the treasuries as mint-constrained token accounts, so a wallet can no longer be stored where a token account belongs), was upgraded in place, and FeeConfig now points at the settlement-mint ATAs recorded under feeConfigTreasuryAtas. Proven end to end on devnet: scripts/prove-devnet-escrow-release.ts ran a real create-vault -> deposit -> reserve -> create/fund escrow -> approve -> release cycle and asserted the exact 15 bps fee reaching all four treasuries at the 40/30/20/10 split (release signature 5o7Qk11e4yniEzrT8CesCZCCDQf5aVjt1DHCSqNcFqgwZkEz4gp2T1sQNTrnDZTdTSQezt5on3V1f1TUJEqs5tsF). The ATAs are for the devnet settlement (USDC) mint, NOT the OPEN mint: the settlement fee is a slice of the traded amount and is moved by transfer_checked out of the trade's own escrow vault, so treasuries must hold the mint trades settle in. One FeeConfig carries one treasury set, so fee collection currently supports a single settlement mint; a second traded stablecoin needs per-mint treasuries.

stakingAuthorities.note: Corrected by the staking program's new admin-only `update_staking_config`, applied on devnet in 2epNWu1sWqugMLRHwEvof6foAKzR1QZYD5CYeqg8Rxga45upPwcZjGDzRCg2nrkSL16jX7hAkGRNgyoP2e2gRtQK. ONE field was broken, not two. `slash_destination` held HLEB5akyStXEZfsTtgpnzexC4gyvDS5QNiYm1vDSHX4p, an address with NO ACCOUNT AT ALL on devnet, while `slash` requires that key to deserialize as a Token-2022 TokenAccount — so every slash failed at account load and the whole disincentive half of the arbitration incentive was dead code. Nothing rejected the value at write time because `initialize_staking_config` takes it as a plain Pubkey, the same class of defect that made release_escrow unexecutable until update_fee_config fixed it. The new instruction takes the destination as a mint-constrained token account, so neither a wallet nor a nonexistent address can be stored there again, and it rejects a zero authority.
stakingAuthorities.slashDestinationRationale: The emergency reserve owner's Token-2022 ATA for the OPEN mint. OPEN, not USDC: slashed tokens leave the stake vault, which is OPEN-denominated (verified on-chain), so a USDC fee treasury would fail on a mint mismatch. The emergency reserve rather than development or ecosystem because slashed stake is a forfeiture, not earned revenue — routing penalties into an operational budget would give the protocol a budgetary interest in slashing its own participants. [PROPOSED — NEEDS SIGN-OFF] Routing forfeitures to the arbitration pool instead, so honest arbitrators are paid by dishonest ones, is arguably better aligned but is a design change: the pool is a per-case PDA funded by merchant deposits, with no single global account to route to.
stakingAuthorities.rewardsAuthorityNote: EA8TyQ58... — unchanged by this update, and already correct. It does concentrate reward distribution on a single EOA, the same centralisation point crates/rewards documents for the cranker, recorded here so it is a known property rather than a later discovery. Governance-controlled distribution is the eventual answer and is deliberately not this change. Note the program takes both authorities as plain Pubkeys rather than requiring them to sign: a signature would prove at write time that somebody holds the key, but a PDA cannot sign a client transaction, and that rule would foreclose ever handing either authority to a program.

misconductCodes.note: [PROPOSED — NEEDS SIGN-OFF] OFS-4100 §4 enumerates the slashing triggers but assigns them no codes. 1 = revealed vote outside dispute consensus (OFS-2400 §328), emitted by the relay in crates/slashing.

governanceForfeitDestination.note: FIXED. GovernanceConfig.forfeit_destination held VueuQemTWZcZXMhfN1jRH1vs1zeWXYvzhDPC8uxJARF — the ecosystem treasury *owner* wallet, not a token account. This is the same class of defect as the FeeConfig treasuries and staking's slash_destination: initialize_governance_config takes the field as a plain Pubkey, so nothing rejected a wallet at write time. The impact was wider than the field's name suggests. refund_or_forfeit_deposit loads forfeit_destination as a Token-2022 TokenAccount in its *account context*, before the handler chooses a branch, so account loading failed on every call — REFUNDS TOO, not just forfeitures. A proposal's deposit could never be settled either way, in either direction. The governance program gained an admin-gated `update_governance_config` which takes the destination as a mint-constrained token account (and additionally requires governance_config.mint == mint, since GovernanceConfig records its own mint), so neither a wallet nor a wrong-mint account can be stored there again.
governanceForfeitDestination.forfeitDestinationRationale: [PROPOSED — NEEDS SIGN-OFF] The ecosystem treasury owner's Token-2022 ATA for the OPEN mint. OPEN, not USDC: the governance deposit vault is OPEN-denominated, so a USDC treasury would fail on a mint mismatch. The owner is deliberately unchanged from the wallet the config already named — the stored value recorded where forfeited deposits were meant to go, so this corrects the type error without quietly relocating protocol income. CONSIDERED AND DECIDED THE OTHER WAY: slashDestination above routes forfeitures to the emergency reserve on the reasoning that penalties should not fund an operational budget, or the protocol acquires a budgetary interest in punishing its own participants. A forfeited proposal deposit is arguably the same class of forfeiture and the same argument applies. It was weighed and decided for the ecosystem treasury for now, on the grounds that deposit forfeiture is triggered by a token-weighted vote missing quorum rather than by an authority with a budget, which weakens (but does not eliminate) the incentive concern. Recorded here so the argument does not have to be rediscovered.
governanceForfeitDestination.appliedOnDevnet: Governance program upgraded IN PLACE at AVJfKUjHsizkGGUy8sdz4Xma2hVgmgvgg8GmUMs8E4eE in 3s4voNqyWhyPs3633j9zZZRMdGtXiqBUH9L5GFbfzW5SjU9VuN9yiZQ6TwcFKq5DF5ZBFBm1p7JYUauNd1Nw2V7Q, then update_governance_config applied to governance_config CQJG481GTPh7x6Y3eL39753tFDwChQQVzZ8mNrXKZTSq in 3GHt7uzztRzNeXUmpMcKsypmXahQC9AkTxRwv5AGifbXHXbeo4j5FAfovWdnNdzUN8pMEs1hznDhxJmVqJNDFUbv, via scripts/fix-devnet-governance-forfeit.ts. The deployed bytes were dumped back and sha256-compared to the tested binary (d2ecfb7eb1e86cebd776f3b3d301bd5c0d9935cb540f32ffb62f1c6b88c097e1, identical after trimming the all-zero padding to the account's 352248-byte capacity). Verified after: every numeric field read off the live account and written back unchanged, then re-decoded — total_open_supply=1000000000000000000, quorum_bps=1000, threshold_simple_bps=5001, threshold_treasury_bps=6000, threshold_upgrade_bps=6600, quorum_upgrade_bps=2000, deposit_amount=5000000000000, vote_lock_secs=604800, all identical before and after; only forfeit_destination moved.
governanceForfeitDestination.decodeDiscipline: OFS-4200 §7.1. The script decodes GovernanceConfig with a single moving cursor and asserts the walk consumes exactly the account length minus its two trailing u8 bumps (138 of 140 bytes). This is not ceremony: an earlier StakingConfig decode in this repo used independently-computed per-field offsets, skipped a 32-byte field, and reported two adjacent pubkeys with their identities transposed — both well-formed, both wrong, and it read as correct until the chain contradicted it. A cursor that must balance cannot skip a field silently. The decoded values are also individually recognisable (5001 bps, 5000 OPEN at 9 decimals, 604800s), which catches a transposition that a balanced walk alone would not.
governanceForfeitDestination.depositVaultBalanceAtFix: 0 — no deposit had ever been taken, so the correction is forward-looking and there was no stranded balance to migrate.

feeConfigTreasuryAtas.note: Token-2022 associated token accounts for the devnet settlement (USDC) mint SK1JEbfsjjTG2WELNirmM7iJVcdnwerqfF32kCnoWsM, owned by the four wallets above. These are what FeeConfig actually stores now. Created and wired by scripts/init-devnet-fee-treasuries.ts.

devnet_programs.note: Deployed via `solana program deploy --url devnet` and initialized via a one-off script using the new Rust SDK's onchain::{escrow,staking,governance} builders (Phase 8's own deploy+init step, pulled forward from Phase 9's original schedule — Phase 8's app wiring needs a real devnet deployment to cut over against). FeeConfig/StakingConfig/GovernanceConfig singletons are all live: staking_config.mint = governance_config.mint = the real devnet OPEN mint above (decimals 9); staking's unbonding/slash_bps and governance's quorum/threshold/deposit/vote_lock all use OFS-4100's own recommended [PROPOSED — NEEDS SIGN-OFF] figures, not invented values. LAYOUT CHANGE: StakingConfig's flat min_stake plus special-cased min_stake_arbitrator were replaced by a per-role min_stake_by_role array ([u64; 7], indexed by Role), and the minimums are now actually enforced by `stake` and `request_unstake` — previously they were stored and read by nothing, so any amount was accepted. The already-deployed config account was rewritten in place by the program's own `migrate_staking_config` instruction (scripts/migrate-devnet-staking-config.ts) rather than being recreated, so the config PDA and both token vaults kept their addresses. Live values: 1,000 OPEN for every role except Arbitrator at 10,000 (both per OFS-4100 §4) and NotificationProvider at 5,000 (protocol-steward decision; OFS-4100 §4 amended to record it).

disputeParameters.note: Dispute-case parameters introduced with the arbitration security fix. All three are [PROPOSED — NEEDS SIGN-OFF]: they are economic/liveness choices, not values any spec fixes. commitDisputeVote is now gated on the committer holding the Arbitrator role's minimum stake (min_stake_by_role[Arbitrator], currently 10,000 OPEN) — previously any wallet could commit, and since initialize_stake_account is permissionless and a zero balance is legal, seven throwaway wallets could occupy all MAX_ARBITRATORS seats for the price of rent, reveal zero-weight votes, and drive the tally to an all-zero tie that resolved to InvalidDispute, returning the escrow to the seller. A merchant could keep a buyer's money after the buyer had sent fiat. The tally now also skips zero-weight reveals, and an undecided round no longer pays anyone: it re-opens the case, bounded by maxDisputeRounds, after which the escrow splits evenly so neither side profits from forcing indecision. MutualSettlement likewise splits evenly rather than falling into the merchant-wins arm as it previously did; a ratio-bearing partial settlement (OFS-2400 §17) remains future work. minDisputeWindowSecs is deliberately low — it is a liveness guard against a same-block window, not the anti-squatting defence, which is the stake gate; a production floor should reflect real arbitrator discovery latency over gossip.
disputeParameters.undecidedRoundPolicy: re-open the case; split the escrow evenly once maxDisputeRounds is reached
disputeParameters.settlementFeeOnEvenSplit: none — the protocol did not successfully arbitrate

rewardsAndFees.note: OFS-4100 §9 implementation. Three fees with three payers, each now with an identified source of funds: the BUYER bears the settlement fee (deducted from the escrowed amount at release, in the traded stablecoin); the MERCHANT bears the ad-listing fee (charge_ad_listing_fee, debited from their OPEN liquidity vault) and the arbitration deposit (open_dispute_case, also from their OPEN vault, whoever opened the case). Before this, ad_listing_fee and dispute_filing_fee were stored on FeeConfig and read by no instruction, and no instruction funded the staking rewards vault, so no reward was ever payable.
rewardsAndFees.settlementFeeBpsStatus: [DECISION — protocol steward] 0.85%, superseding the 15 bps originally deployed. Governance-updatable via update_fee_config.
rewardsAndFees.arbitrationPoolNote: Singleton OPEN token account owned by the FeeConfig PDA, created by initialize_arbitration_pool. Deliberately NOT one of the four settlement-fee treasuries: those are external wallet-owned accounts routing revenue, whereas this holds funds still owed either back to a merchant or forward to arbitrators. Mixing a liability with revenue would make neither auditable.
proposedNeedsSignOff: Arbitration deposit disposition when the merchant WINS or the outcome is InvalidDispute: returned to the merchant's OPEN vault. The steward specified forfeiture only for 'merchant loses'; 'deposit' ordinarily implies return when not at fault, but this was not stated.

Arbitration deposit disposition at the MAX_DISPUTE_ROUNDS terminal even split (no consensus, no loser): returned to the merchant's OPEN vault. Forfeiting on 'nobody reached consensus' would punish a merchant for an outcome the arbitrators failed to produce.
Arbitration deposit disposition on MutualSettlement: returned, same reasoning — neither side was found at fault.

Partial/zero deposit collection when the merchant's OPEN vault cannot cover the fee: the case opens anyway with whatever was available, and the shortfall is recorded in the ArbitrationDepositTaken event. Requiring the full deposit would let a merchant make themselves undisputable by keeping their OPEN vault empty, which is a far worse failure than one case's arbitrators going unpaid.
Ad-listing fee destination: the development treasury. OFS-4100 §6 sets the fee's amount but names no destination, and splitting a small flat charge four ways would add four accounts to every listing.

Ad-listing fee charged via a dedicated instruction rather than at vault creation, deposit, or reservation: a merchant funds once but lists many times, and charging at reservation would bill per trade, which is the settlement fee's job.
rewardsAndFees.slashBelowMinimumNote: slash may now leave a balance below the role minimum, and deliberately does. Sweeping the remainder to zero would also restore the 'non-zero stake is a qualifying stake' invariant, but it turns a slash_bps penalty into total forfeiture for anyone staked at the minimum — the common case for arbitrators, and contrary to OFS-2400 §16's 'partial, moderate stake slash'. The invariant is instead enforced in StakeAccount::effective_stake, which returns 0 below the minimum, so governance vote weight and the dispute tally both ignore such an account while it keeps its tokens.
rewardsAndFees.eventsNote: The programs workspace previously contained zero emit!/#[event]. Reward, claim, slash, vault-funding, escrow-release (with the full four-way fee split), dispute-resolution, deposit-taken and reward-claim events are now emitted so an indexer can rebuild history from logs alone (OFS-4100 §9.4).

banList.spec: OFS-7100 §12 — the protocol-enforced ban list. A wallet on the list cannot deposit into any vault; enforcement is in the programs, not in each application.
banList.authority: ADMIN-GATED, NOT GOVERNANCE-EXECUTED. [PROPOSED — NEEDS SIGN-OFF] §12.2 says only governance may add or remove entries. That is NOT what is deployed. list_wallet/delist_wallet check GovernanceConfig.admin — a single key, EA8TyQ58C3eavg3ThRFTMu1KLyV9e1v2oTQubSBQ9s5z — and consult no proposal, vote, or quorum. This is not a shortcut taken in these two instructions; it is a missing capability in the program. update_config_parameter and authorize_treasury_spend, the two instructions an accepted proposal is meant to act through, only set Proposal.executed = true and return: they record an authorization, they never perform one. No accepted proposal can cause any state change anywhere today, so gating the ban list on a proposal would have gated it on machinery that cannot fire. The honest statement of the power now deployed is: one key can deny any wallet deposit access to the entire protocol, and the same key can restore it. Do not describe the ban list as governance-controlled in any app, doc, or explorer surface until the item under `remainingWorkForGovernanceControl` is done.
banList.remainingWorkForGovernanceControl: An execution path that lets a finalized Proposal authorize a state change — a proposal-signed PDA authority, or an execute_proposal instruction that verifies state == Accepted && quorum_met && !executed and CPIs into the target — and then re-gating list_wallet AND delist_wallet on that instead of on admin. Both, together: an authority that can exclude but not readmit is the specific failure §12.2 names, and §15's false-positive handling depends on readmission being at least as available as exclusion.

record.fields: wallet, reason (StolenFunds|Sanctions|Phishing|Scam|Other), evidence_hash, listed_at, listed_by, bump
record.readableOnChain: Yes — §12.2 requires it. reason and evidence_hash are stored so a listing can be audited and contested against a fixed artefact, not just enforced.
record.events: WalletListed on list_wallet, WalletDelisted on delist_wallet — both required by §12.2. WalletDelisted carries the original listed_at, because the record that knew it is closed by the time the event is read.

enforcement.mechanism: Proof of non-existence. Each gated instruction takes the canonical ban address for ITS OWN SIGNER as an UncheckedAccount constrained by seeds = [BAN_SEED, signer], seeds::program = GOVERNANCE_PROGRAM_ID, and requires it to be unoccupied. A wallet is banned iff that address holds an account.
enforcement.whyTheConstraintIsTheWholeProperty: Anchor re-derives the address from the signer's key and rejects a mismatch. Without that, a banned caller would pass any unrelated empty account and the emptiness check would pass them — the gate would be decorative. Two tests cover this directly: an unrelated empty account is rejected, and so is another wallet's real, genuinely-empty ban PDA. Both fail with ConstraintSeeds.
enforcement.sharedImplementation: BAN_SEED, GOVERNANCE_PROGRAM_ID and wallet_is_banned live in openfiat-programs-shared, not in the governance crate. escrow/staking/presale cannot depend on governance — governance already depends on staking to weigh votes, so staking -> governance would close a dependency cycle. The gate needs only two constants because it never deserializes a BanRecord, so the shared crate breaks the cycle and gives all four programs one implementation instead of four hand-copied ones. governance asserts its declare_id! equals the shared constant in a unit test; a divergence would silently disable every gate at once without failing any build.

gatedInstructions.escrow::deposit_liquidity: Merchant ATA -> liquidity vault. A deposit into a vault.
gatedInstructions.staking::stake: Owner ATA -> stake vault. A deposit into a vault.
gatedInstructions.staking::fund_rewards_vault: Funder ATA -> rewards vault. See fundRewardsVaultDecision below — this one is a genuine judgement call.
gatedInstructions.governance::create_proposal: Proposer ATA -> deposit vault. A deposit into a vault.
gatedInstructions.presale::contribute_usdc: Buyer ATA -> presale usdc_vault. A deposit into a vault.
gatedInstructions.presale::contribute_with_swap: Buyer's SOL/whitelisted stablecoin -> presale usdc_vault via a swap CPI. Same deposit through a different door.

notGatedAndWhy.escrow::fund_trade_escrow: NOT GATED, and this is a departure from the original brief, which listed it. Its `from` is liquidity_token_vault — a protocol-owned PDA, not the merchant's wallet. The tokens are already inside the protocol; they entered through deposit_liquidity, which IS gated. Gating it would not stop a deposit, it would strand already-deposited liquidity mid-trade, and it would break a counterparty buyer who had already committed to the trade because of the merchant's status. That is confiscation and collateral damage, not exclusion.
notGatedAndWhy.escrow::charge_ad_listing_fee, escrow::o: NOT GATED. Both debit the merchant's already-funded OPEN liquidity vault (a PDA), not a wallet. Same reasoning as fund_trade_escrow.
notGatedAndWhy.withdrawal and payout paths: NOT GATED: escrow::withdraw_liquidity, escrow::claim_arbitration_reward, staking::request_unstake, staking::withdraw_unstaked, staking::claim_rewards, presale::claim, presale::refund. §12 excludes banned wallets from depositing, not from recovering what they already deposited. Gating these would be seizure of existing balances, which §12 does not authorize and which no delisting could undo if the funds had meanwhile been swept. The Rust SDK carries an explicit test (request_unstake_carries_no_ban_gate) so an accidental gate here fails CI rather than silently seizing.
notGatedAndWhy.authority-driven and permissionless path: NOT GATED: staking::slash (slashing authority), presale::finalize_sale (admin), escrow::execute_dispute_outcome and governance::refund_or_forfeit_deposit (no signer at all — nothing to check a ban against).

banList.gateListVsBrief: The brief supplied five instructions and asked for them to be verified. Result: one removed (escrow::fund_trade_escrow, vault-to-vault, see above) and two added (presale::contribute_usdc and presale::contribute_with_swap). contribute_with_swap is the important addition: it moves funds into the presale vault entirely through a swap CPI and contains no transfer_checked of its own, so it does not appear in a transfer-site inventory at all. Gating contribute_usdc while leaving it open would have left the presale gate bypassable by routing the same contribution through the swap path.
banList.fundRewardsVaultDecision: GATED, and it was close. The argument against: it is a one-way donation. The funder gets no stake account, no claim, no receipt, no position — refusing it denies the banned party nothing they wanted and costs the protocol a donation, so the gate looks like it punishes the protocol more than the listed wallet. The argument that won: accepting it means knowingly taking tokens from a wallet governance has declared stolen or sanctioned and distributing them to honest stakers, who cannot refuse the taint and had no part in the decision. Pushing the contamination onto uninvolved third parties is worse than declining a donation nobody was counting on — realistically the rewards pool is funded by protocol fee flows, not by walk-up donors, so the expected cost of refusing is about zero. Secondary: §12 says 'any vault' without exception, and the rewards vault is a vault; carving out the first exception invites the same argument for the next one. Limitation, stated plainly: the gate is not a laundering defence. A determined actor donates from a fresh unbanned wallet. What it buys is that the protocol does not KNOWINGLY accept from a wallet it has itself listed.
banList.clientBreakingChange: Adding an account to an instruction's Accounts struct changes its wire format. Any client that builds deposit_liquidity, stake, fund_rewards_vault, create_proposal, contribute_usdc or contribute_with_swap by hand must add the ban_record account in the position shown in the regenerated IDL (immediately after the signer) or the instruction fails. Clients using Anchor's IDL-driven resolution need no change — the IDL carries the full PDA derivation including seeds::program, so ban_record resolves automatically. The Rust and TypeScript SDK builders in openfiat-sdks were updated.

deployedOnDevnet.summary: All four programs upgraded IN PLACE at their existing ids on 2026-07-29 — no program id changed, no keypair was needed (the deploy keypairs were destroyed by an earlier cargo clean; upgrade authority EA8TyQ58C3eavg3ThRFTMu1KLyV9e1v2oTQubSBQ9s5z is the only path and was used for all four). Deployed incrementally, smallest first, each verified before the next.
deployedOnDevnet.orderAndWhyItIsSafe: staking, presale, governance, escrow. Partial deployment is safe in either direction and was not a risk taken blindly: the gate reads an address under the governance program id, so an upgraded escrow/staking/presale simply sees an always-empty address until governance gains list_wallet (every wallet reads as unbanned), and an upgraded governance with un-upgraded enforcers can list a wallet that is not yet refused. Neither state is inconsistent; both are merely incomplete. escrow went last because at 687,488 bytes its deploy buffer needs ~4.8 SOL against a 5.47 SOL balance.
deployedOnDevnet.governanceExtend: governance needed `solana program extend` before it would fit: the new binary is 368,240 bytes against a 352,248-byte data account. Extended by 24,576 bytes (15,992 required, the rest headroom) to 376,824. The other three fit their existing capacity unchanged.
deployedOnDevnet.byteVerification: Each program's deployed bytes were dumped back with `solana program dump` and sha256-compared to the exact binary the test suite ran against. A dump is padded to the account's capacity, so the padding tail was asserted to be all zeros BEFORE trimming to the local length — trimming first would make any tail compare equal and prove nothing. All four matched: escrow 6d1df7cff65ec6b2a252a2f3d030ff94596c212e2fae8d64948aa356ae49b405 (27,160 zero bytes of padding), staking c269205c9b6f31ed262ff62cab90516ee599e7b3efdac24a0f182af23b211362 (7,272), governance f6a7dd86909220badc3cce44a6aea71c8a9f0ff34a7239cf12e235649b8568da (8,584), presale 2bfa0d63095f8f7cae675d60202713be70f637f085a3a05a850b4b720090fd8b (7,592).
deployedOnDevnet.testedBinaryDiscipline: The suite was re-run against the final binaries rather than an earlier build. A doc-comment edit to fund_rewards_vault after the first green run changed staking.so's hash (Anchor embeds doc strings in the IDL), so the first run had not exercised the bytes that would ship. Re-running cost 16 minutes and removed the need to assert 'it was only a comment'. 83 passing both times.
deployedOnDevnet.liveProof: scripts/prove-devnet-ban-list.ts, run against devnet after deployment. It asserts, in order: GovernanceConfig still decodes with a balanced field-by-field walk (OFS-4200 §7.1, cursor must land exactly at length-2 for the two trailing bumps) and every stored value is unchanged by the upgrade; list_wallet creates a readable BanRecord (list 3RpGeptAbvBiooLkUXb9YG7sJTxz8uNL22NpFfChTn8i523fgKPP4yE9K5FUvBodpGj6xWwiLAcKteTXwuw6SErc); the DEPLOYED staking program then refuses that wallet's stake with WalletBanned, which is the cross-program claim §12 makes and which no single-program test can establish; a substituted ban_record — a real, correctly-derived, genuinely-empty ban PDA belonging to a different wallet — is rejected with ConstraintSeeds; and delist_wallet closes the record (4GkThCCucr4cmvp1a9xrpnCviYyN1jBX27SJWe2RFRYJYqTpu9ESdfNq8vMMYTYoKvSe8gTyvRJpfEsWcgH2mzpr) after which the same stake fails with StakeBelowRoleMinimum instead of WalletBanned. That last detail is the point: a DIFFERENT failure proves access was restored, where a repeat of the same error would have proven only that the instruction was broken.
deployedOnDevnet.governanceConfigAfterUpgrade: Unchanged, as expected — this change adds no field to GovernanceConfig, so no realloc was needed and none was done. Read back off chain after the upgrade: admin=EA8TyQ58C3eavg3ThRFTMu1KLyV9e1v2oTQubSBQ9s5z, mint=29w8TroBTYoaqrXBDcpv5L54VZRA8Kf7kU5U1cakvFdj, total_open_supply=1000000000000000000, quorum_bps=1000, threshold_simple_bps=5001, threshold_treasury_bps=6000, threshold_upgrade_bps=6600, quorum_upgrade_bps=2000, deposit_amount=5000000000000, forfeit_destination=H4Ghu6Q3MNzyX59pZ6L7jAjFFa2vR6YUdreLRN755ULF, vote_lock_secs=604800.
deployedOnDevnet.whyBanAuthorityReusesAdminRatherThanANew: A separate ban_authority field was considered and rejected on deployment-safety grounds, not design grounds. GovernanceConfig is a live singleton allocated at its current size; adding a Pubkey would make every load of the account fail to deserialize until a realloc ran, bricking the whole program in the window between. Reusing the existing admin is the same power with no migration. A distinct, separately-delegable ban authority is worth having later, and should arrive with the governance execution path rather than ahead of it.
